title: Carmen Suite No. 1
hook: The opera’s preludes and dances without the singers, from the shadow of fate to the bullfighters’ parade.

painting.title: Spanish Ballet
painting.pairingNote: Dancers from Madrid’s Royal Theatre, painted in Paris during their 1862 season there; like Bizet, who never visited Spain, Manet painted the Spain that Paris was in love with.

facts: *Carmen*, Bizet’s last opera, opened at the Opéra-Comique in Paris on 3 March 1875. It is set in Seville around 1820: Carmen, a Roma woman who works in the cigarette factory, seduces the soldier Don José, leaves him for the bullfighter Escamillo, and is stabbed by José outside the bullring.

The audience was shocked by the story and the reviews were mostly hostile. Bizet died three months later, on 3 June 1875, aged 36, and never knew that within ten years *Carmen* would be played all over the world.

The suite is not by Bizet. After his death his friend Ernest Guiraud assembled concert suites from the opera for its publisher, Choudens; a later German edition by Fritz Hoffmann, with almost the same pieces, is the one usually played. Suite No. 1 takes mostly the orchestral preludes and [[entr-acte|entr’acte]]s, the music the orchestra plays while the curtain is down.
Bizet never went to Spain. He took Spanish dance rhythms and colours from books of songs and from the Spanish fashion in Paris, and made from them music that sounds Spanish to the whole world.
bigPicture.inOneLine: fate and a dance (I), a night in the mountains (II), Carmen’s tease (III), a soldier’s song (IV), the bullfighters’ parade (V).

movements.heading: Prélude – Aragonaise
movements.title: Prélude – Aragonaise
movements.summary: Two pieces in one track. The Prélude is the dark second half of the opera’s overture: the theme of Carmen and her fate, heard over trembling strings, which breaks off on an unresolved chord. Straight after it comes the Aragonaise, the prelude to the last act, a dance from Aragon with a guitar-like strumming and an oboe tune, played while the crowd gathers outside the bullring.

mainIdeas.name: The fate theme
mainIdeas.description: a slow, winding tune with a sinister bend in it, played low by cellos, clarinet, bassoon and cornet over a string [[tremolo|tremolo]].

mainIdeas.name: The Aragonaise
mainIdeas.description: hard, stamping chords, then a lilting oboe melody over plucked strings, harp and tambourine.

stops.hear: Strings shiver softly; low instruments play a slow, winding tune with a menacing twist
stops.happening: The fate theme, the music of Carmen and of her death

stops.hear: The theme climbs higher and louder, with harsher chords
A loud, unresolved chord, then silence
stops.happening: The Prélude breaks off, as in the opera when the curtain rises

stops.hear: Sharp, stamping chords, then plucked strings and harp strumming like guitars, with tambourine
stops.happening: The Aragonaise begins: a Spanish dance in quick three

stops.hear: An oboe plays a long, swaying, ornamented melody over the strumming
The melody passes to other instruments and the whole orchestra grows louder

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The stamping chords and the oboe tune come back, and the dance closes
stops.happening: The curtain is about to rise on the last act

notice: Listen for the moment the Prélude stops. It does not end: it breaks off on a chord that needs an answer, the same tension that hangs over the whole opera.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Charles Dutoit and the Montreal Symphony Orchestra recorded both *Carmen* suites and both *L’Arlésienne* suites in the church of Saint-Eustache, near Montreal, and Decca released them on one disc in 1988. On the Spotify album Suite No. 1 is tracks 9–13; Dutoit’s disc puts the Prélude and the Aragonaise together on one track.

movements.heading: Intermezzo
movements.title: Intermezzo
movements.summary: The prelude to Act III, where the smugglers, with José among them, are camped at night in the mountains. A flute sings a calm, long melody over a harp, and the other woodwinds join one by one. It is the gentlest music in the opera, a moment of peace before the story turns dark.

mainIdeas.name: The flute melody
mainIdeas.description: long, calm phrases over rippling harp chords, later taken up by the clarinet and other woodwinds.

stops.hear: A harp ripples gently; a flute plays a long, calm melody
A clarinet takes the melody while the flute weaves around it
More woodwinds and the strings join, and the sound grows warmer and fuller
The flute returns alone above the harp

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: Soft, sustained chords and a last ripple from the harp

notice: Count the instruments that take the flute’s melody. Each one adds a new colour to the same tune.

movements.heading: Séguedille
movements.title: Séguedille
movements.summary: In Act I Carmen, arrested after a fight in the cigarette factory, has her hands tied and is left in José’s charge. She sings him a seguidilla, an Andalusian dance-song, about the tavern of her friend Lillas Pastia, where she will dance tonight with her lover, whoever he may be. José gives in and lets her escape. In the suite her voice is given to the instruments.

mainIdeas.name: The seguidilla tune
mainIdeas.description: light and teasing, in a quick three, with little hesitations as if Carmen were smiling over her shoulder.

stops.hear: Plucked strings set a light, quick three-beat rhythm; a woodwind plays a teasing, swaying tune
The tune moves to the strings and grows fuller
The opening tune again, then a quickening

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A quick, bright flourish and two short chords

notice: Listen to how the tune keeps pausing and starting again. In the opera, these are the moments where Carmen watches to see whether José is listening.

movements.heading: Les dragons d'Alcala
movements.title: Les dragons d'Alcala
movements.summary: The prelude to Act II. José has gone to prison for letting Carmen escape, and this little march is the song he sings on his way to meet her again: “Halte-là! Qui va là? Dragon d’Alcala!”, the challenge and reply of a soldier of the Alcalá dragoons. Two bassoons play it, side by side, light and a little comic.

mainIdeas.name: The soldier’s song
mainIdeas.description: a short, jaunty march in two bassoons, played crisply and quietly over plucked strings and a soft side drum.

stops.hear: Two bassoons play a short, jaunty march together, over soft plucked strings and a side drum
Clarinets take the tune, a little higher and brighter
The bassoons again, with the rest of the orchestra joining lightly

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The march fades away into quiet
stops.happening: The soldier goes on his way

notice: The bassoons play almost the whole piece quietly, without a single loud climax. Notice how much character Bizet gets from two low instruments walking in step.

movements.heading: Les toréadors
movements.title: Les toréadors
movements.summary: The first, brilliant part of the opera’s overture, with its music for the bullfighters’ procession in the last act. A loud, glittering march with cymbals and triangle frames a famous tune in the middle: the refrain of the toreador Escamillo’s song.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: fast and bright, with crashing cymbals and the whole orchestra in full voice.

mainIdeas.name: The toreador’s refrain
mainIdeas.description: a swaggering melody in the strings, first soft, then loud.

stops.hear: The whole orchestra bursts out with a fast, glittering march, cymbals and triangle ringing
A lighter, quieter strain, then the march again
The strings play a broad, swaggering melody, softly at first, then with the whole orchestra
stops.happening: The refrain of the toreador’s song

stops.hear: The opening march returns

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: Loud, hammered closing chords

notice: You probably know the middle tune. In the opera Escamillo sings it in the tavern in Act II, boasting about the bullring, the crowd and the dark eyes that watch the toreador as he fights.

threads.title: An opera without voices
threads.body: Most of this music is what the orchestra plays while the stage waits: preludes and entr’actes. Heard together, they still tell the story, from the fate theme to the bullring.

threads.title: Fate and festivity
threads.body: The suite opens with the dark theme of fate and ends with the bright parade. In the opera the two are joined: the overture runs straight from the parade into the fate theme.

threads.title: A Paris Spain
threads.body: Spanish rhythms, guitar-like plucking, tambourines and castanet-like patter, all imagined by a composer who never crossed the Pyrenees.
